Li-ion.description: Lithium-ion batteries are the most widely used rechargeable batteries in consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and energy storage systems. They offer high energy density, long cycle life, and low self-discharge rates.
Li-ion.recycling_process: Typically involves mechanical dismantling, thermal pre-treatment, hydrometallurgical leaching (acid dissolution), followed by solvent extraction and precipitation to recover individual metals.
Li-ion.environmental_notes: Contains flammable electrolyte (organic solvents). Must be discharged and handled with care. Cobalt mining has significant environmental and ethical concerns.

Cobalt.process: Recovered through acid leaching and solvent extraction. Cobalt sulfate or cobalt oxide is precipitated for reuse in new cathode production.

Nickel.process: Extracted through hydrometallurgical processes. Nickel sulfate is commonly recovered for cathode precursor manufacturing.

Lithium.process: Recovered as lithium carbonate (Li2CO3) or lithium hydroxide (LiOH) through precipitation from leach solutions. Lab-scale processes achieve 99%+.

Copper.notes: Current collector foils; efficient mechanical separation
Copper.process: Mechanically separated from anode current collector foils. High-purity copper is recovered through electrolytic refining.

Aluminum.process: Separated mechanically from cathode layers. Aluminum is melted and cast into ingots for reuse.

Graphite.notes: Anode material; reused in new anode production; variable recovery
Graphite.process: Recovered through flotation or thermal treatment. Can be directly reused in new anode production or processed into synthetic graphite.

Manganese.notes: Present in NMC and LMO chemistries
Manganese.process: Co-extracted during hydrometallurgical processing of cathode materials. Recovered as manganese sulfate or MnO2.

LiFePO4.description: LiFePO4 batteries are known for superior thermal stability, long cycle life (2000+ cycles), and safety. They are cobalt-free, making them more environmentally friendly than standard Li-ion.
LiFePO4.recycling_process: Mechanical shredding and classification, followed by hydrometallurgical treatment. Iron phosphate can be re-synthesized directly into new LFP cathode material.
LiFePO4.environmental_notes: Considered safer than other lithium-ion chemistries due to cobalt-free design. Lower thermal runaway risk. Iron and phosphate are non-toxic.

Lithium.notes: Carbonate or hydroxide form; precipitation method
Lithium.process: Leached from cathode with dilute acids and precipitated as lithium carbonate or lithium hydroxide for reuse.

Iron.process: Recovered as iron phosphate (FePO4) which can be directly re-synthesized into LFP cathode material, creating a closed-loop process.

Phosphate.notes: Can be re-synthesized into LFP cathode material
Phosphate.process: Co-recovered with iron through selective leaching. Phosphate is re-used in cathode synthesis or as fertilizer feedstock.

Copper.process: Separated from anode current collector foils via mechanical processing and electrolytic refining.

Aluminum.process: Mechanical separation and smelting. Aluminum casing and cathode foils are collected separately.

Carbon (Graphite).process: Flotation and thermal purification. Graphite can be regenerated for reuse as anode material in new battery cells.

NiMH.description: NiMH batteries are widely used rechargeable alternatives to single-use alkaline batteries. They offer good capacity, are less toxic than NiCd, and are commonly found in hybrid vehicles and consumer electronics.
NiMH.recycling_process: Pyrometallurgical smelting at high temperatures to recover nickel and cobalt as alloy. Rare earth elements are recovered through hydrometallurgical acid leaching.
NiMH.environmental_notes: Relatively low toxicity. Contains rare earth elements (La, Ce, Nd) whose mining has significant environmental impact. Nickel recovery is economically viable.

Nickel.process: Recovered through pyrometallurgical smelting. Nickel is the most economically valuable component and drives recycling economics.

Cobalt.process: Co-recovered with nickel during smelting. Separated through solvent extraction in downstream processing.

Rare Earth Elements.notes: La, Ce, Nd in anode alloy; specialized hydromet process required
Rare Earth Elements.process: Lanthanum, cerium, and neodymium are recovered from the hydrogen-absorbing anode alloy via acid leaching and selective precipitation.

Iron.process: Steel casing is separated magnetically and melted for scrap steel production.

Zinc.process: Recovered through hydrometallurgical processing of the anode alloy. Zinc is precipitated as zinc oxide or zinc sulfate.

NiCd.description: NiCd batteries offer excellent high-drain performance and long shelf life. However, they contain toxic cadmium and are being phased out in many regions due to EU Battery Directive restrictions.
NiCd.recycling_process: Vacuum thermal distillation to recover cadmium as vapour (mandatory by law). Nickel is recovered through pyrometallurgical smelting. Steel casing is magnetically separated.
NiCd.environmental_notes: ⚠️ CADMIUM IS HIGHLY TOXIC — mandatory recycling in EU/US. Cadmium is a carcinogen and persistent environmental pollutant. Strict handling and processing regulations apply.

Cadmium.notes: TOXIC — mandatory recovery; vacuum thermal distillation
Cadmium.process: Recovered via vacuum thermal distillation at 767°C. Cadmium vapour is condensed and cast into ingots. Recovery is mandatory under EU Battery Directive.

Nickel.process: After cadmium removal, nickel-rich residue is smelted in electric arc furnaces to produce ferronickel alloy.

Steel.process: Steel casing is magnetically separated during initial dismantling and sent to scrap metal recycling.

Potassium Hydroxide.process: Alkaline electrolyte is drained and neutralized to potassium sulfate, which can be used as fertilizer.

Lead-Acid.description: Lead-acid batteries are the most recycled consumer product globally, with over 99% recycling rates in developed countries. They are used primarily in automotive starting, lighting, and ignition (SLI) systems and UPS backup.
Lead-Acid.recycling_process: Batteries are drained of acid, crushed, and separated into lead, plastic (polypropylene), and acid fractions. Lead is smelted in blast or rotary furnaces. Plastic is reprocessed into new casings.
Lead-Acid.environmental_notes: ⚠️ LEAD IS TOXIC — regulated hazardous waste. Despite toxicity, lead-acid has the highest recycling rate of any battery type. Acid must be neutralized or converted before disposal.

Lead.process: Lead plates, paste, and grid alloys are smelted in rotary or blast furnaces. Secondary lead accounts for 80% of global lead production.

Sulfuric Acid.notes: Neutralized or converted to sodium sulfate for industrial use
Sulfuric Acid.process: Acid is either neutralized to sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) for use in detergent and glass manufacturing, or purified and reused in new batteries.

Polypropylene.notes: Plastic casing; reprocessed into new battery cases
Polypropylene.process: Polypropylene casings are washed, shredded, and pelletized. The recycled PP is directly reused to manufacture new battery casings.

Antimony.notes: Grid alloy component; recovered during smelting
Antimony.process: Co-recovered with lead during smelting. Antimony is separated and reused as a lead-grid hardening agent in new batteries.

Alkaline.description: Alkaline batteries are the most common primary (non-rechargeable) battery type used globally. They power everyday devices and are produced in billions annually. Recycling is growing in importance.
Alkaline.recycling_process: Mechanical shredding and classification. Steel casing is magnetically separated. Zinc and manganese fractions are recovered through pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical processing.
Alkaline.environmental_notes: Mercury-free since the 1990s, making them relatively safe. Zinc and manganese are non-toxic. Some jurisdictions allow landfill disposal, but recycling is recommended for resource conservation.

Zinc.process: Zinc is recovered through pyrometallurgical processing (rotary kiln) or hydrometallurgical acid leaching. Used in galvanizing and zinc oxide production.

Manganese Dioxide.notes: Cathode; reused in pigments, fertilizers, soil amendment
Manganese Dioxide.process: Recovered as manganese oxide through thermal processing. Reused in production of ferromanganese, fertilizers, and as soil micronutrient.

Steel.process: Steel casings are magnetically separated during initial shredding and sent to steel mills for smelting into new products.

Potassium Hydroxide.process: Alkaline electrolyte is washed out and neutralized. Potassium salts may be recovered for industrial use or agricultural applications.
